Charles says slavery history 'fills my heart with horror' - but he avoids apology, and stresses 'evil need not have last word'
Charles carries on with his remarks about history. (See 2.50pm.) Turning to the slave trade, he does not issue an apology – but he says slavery history “fills my heart with horror”, and he stresses the importance of addressing the “wrongs of the past”.
Our history inspires us, can appal us, yet it can always teach us. We cannot change the actions of those who came before us. We can, however, learn from the past.
The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands, and other members of our Commonwealth.
As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow.
And yet, history also teaches us that evil need not have the last word, that character and courage can combine to overcome the most monstrous injustice, as they did with the determination to end the international trade in enslaved people, in which the Royal Navy played such a leading role.
The more I have furthered my own understanding of the issues through listening, learning and looking, the more committed I have become to finding ways for us to work in modern partnership to address the wrongs of the past – with action for the future through improving access to education, investing in jobs and opportunities, encouraging intra-commonwealth trade, and inspiring vital climate resilience measures across the world.
I have always felt that there is so much that can be done to help lift up those who struggle against hardship and disadvantage.
I have always tried to play my part in doing just that. For as any sailor navigating the seas knows, we cannot command the winds, least of all where the winds of yesterday have delivered us. But we can choose how we set our sails.
The British and Australian governments have backed a joint agreement at the Commonwealth summit on working together to tackle threats directed at parliamentarians, especially women. Here is an extract.
We commit to working together with the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association, with the Commonwealth Women Parliamentarians, and with countries from across the Commonwealth to bring together technology, expertise and practical solutions to help protect parliamentarians from online abuse and support democratic participation across the Commonwealth. We’ll hold the first forum in 2027 and will engage all those in the Commonwealth who share these values.
There are a range of software tools that are being trialled in our parliaments and around the world, and we welcome and encourage this innovation.
While we work to change attitudes, restore respectful debate and return people’s choice, in the short term we can commit to take steps together to protect our democracies.
MSPs call for review of law allowing people with just temporary rights to be living in Scotland to be elected to Holyrood
Severin Carrell
Severin Carrell is the Guardian’s Scotland editor.
MSPs at Holyrood have called on Scottish ministers to review a law which allowed the Indian-born student Q Manivannan to win a seat at Holyrood in May, claiming public confidence in parliament was “fragile”.
The standards, procedures and public appointments committee said in a report that the rationale for allowing people with limited rights to be in the UK was “simply not clear” and had “run ahead of what the public want”.
Under the Scottish Elections (Representation and Reform) Act 2025, overseas citizens with the legal right to live in Scotland can stand for Holyrood and local councils, even if their rights are temporary.
There was an outcry led by the Conservatives and Reform UK in May when Manivannan was elected as a Scottish Greens list MSP for Edinburgh and Lothians East. A successful PhD candidate at St Andrews, it emerged their student visa was due to expire at the end of 2026. They have since been granted a three-year graduate visa, giving them right to remain until the end of 2029.
Jenny Minto, the Scottish National party MSP who chairs the committee, and who voted in favour of the reforms last year, said public sentiment appears to have swung against the policy. She said:
It is vital that Scotland has elected representatives who look like the communities they represent. This diversity helps build trust in our elected institutions.
But we know that this trust is fragile, and so careful consideration needs to be given to all electoral reform that comes before us.
Reform UK was delighted by the committee’s recommendation, which follows proposals by ministers to extend the right to Commonwealth citizens, but the Scottish Greens said it was regressive. The Scottish Greens said:
There are thousands of people with limited leave to remain who live and work in Scotland and have made a home here, including Commonwealth citizens. They should be able to stand for our parliament and councils.
MSPs backed this change unanimously at the time, including the convenor and deputy convenor of the committee. It would be a regrettable backwards step for representation and democracy if Scotland was to roll back on this commitment.
Burnham claims he cares less about criticism from newspapers than previous PMs did
Andy Burnham has said that he cares less about what the newspapers say about him than previous prime ministers did.
In one of his interviews with Daniel Hewitt for the ITV documentary being shown tonight about his first 100 days in office, Burnham was asked if he cared less about what papers like the Daily Mail and the Sun said about him than some of his predecessors did. Burnham replied: “Definitely.”
He said:
I left Westminster for a reason. I got fed up with commentators deciding things down there and then the whole world [being] meant to believe what they believe. Well, sorry, the world’s not like that anymore.
Burnham also defended prioritising social media more instead. He said:
People want more involvement, more understanding of the way politics is being done and that’s what I’m bringing. And hopefully it connects with people, particularly younger people, who may have felt quite distant from politics.
In another interview for the programme, Burnham rejected the suggestion that he was ruthless. Explaining why he did not like the description, he said:
Determined, I definitely would say that [I am] determined. I will come back and back and back at something. I’ve always been like that. Ruthless to me says you just have a disregard for everybody else. And that wouldn’t be me. But I am determined.
Burnham also revealed that, since becoming PM, he continues to go running regularly – and that this is often when his “best thoughts” occur. He explained:
If you’re asking me about what’s the thing that makes it work, I go running and I’ve not stopped my running. It’s when my mind goes a bit into neutral. And I feel then I get my best thoughts in those moments.
You know, all of a sudden, "Oh, that, yeah, I’ll do that.’ Or a particularly intractable problem that you’ve been thinking and worrying about – all of a sudden, I’ve been out on a run sometimes, and you just think, ‘Ah, that’s the way I’ll go into that one.’
Reform UK councillor charged with 12 counts of rape and multiple other offences
Reform UK’s leader on Hampshire county council has been charged with 12 counts of rape and one of distributing indecent images of a child, Peter Walker reports.
Charles ended his speech urging Commonwealth leaders to “recommit … to a Commonwealth in which our young people can look to the future with greater confidence and purpose”.
Charles said he was glad climate proposals were being considered at Chogm.
Here in the Caribbean, as in so many parts of our Commonwealth, climate change is not some distant prospect. It is an alarming reality.
As we know, large ocean states have contributed little to the causes of climate change, and yet they are among those bearing the greatest cost.
If we mobilise climate finance through the private sector and with the leveraging capacity of the public sector, we can drive investment into climate resilience.
Nature herself is an essential form of capital that sustains our prosperity and well-being. And yet we have persisted for too long to live off nature’s capital, rather than her income.
To restore nature is therefore not to choose our environment over our economy. It is to invest in the very foundations of our economy, not to mention our security.
Charles said Commonwealth values have never been more important.
What unites this extraordinary and unique group of countries even more deeply is our values of democracy and the rule of law, of respect, equal dignity and human rights, of sustainable development, of peace and security. These values have never been more important, contested as they are on so many fronts, and they guide us to action.
Charles says Commonwealth can draw on 'collective ingenuity of third of humanity' to address problems creating global crisis
Charles says the need for the Commonwealth is “more compelling than ever”.
All around us, trust between nations is under critical strain as international norms and systems are tested to their limits.
Brutal conflict stalks our world, destroying lives and casting long shadows across the globe.
Technology is transforming our societies and our economies at dizzying speed, with little certainty about where it might lead us.
As I consistently tried to emphasise, climate change is no longer just a terrifying prospect, but a catastrophic reality which threatens our very way of life. Nature is under constant attack and critical natural systems are collapsing.
And in each of our countries, for too many people, the opportunity to fulfil their own potential lies far beyond their reach.
Each of these challenges, each of these, is a challenge of the highest order. Together, they comprise the crisis of our time.
The Commonwealth cannot provide all of the solutions. It does, however, offer an unparalleled opportunity to work together across our societies and our economies, through our businesses, our institutions and our communities.
It allows us to draw on the collective ingenuity of a third of humanity to address the challenges confronting us all.

Charles says they are all their because of their history.
None of us, of course, would be here today were it not for our history, which has shaped us in myriad ways.
History is not ours to choose or to change. It is bequeathed to us in complex synthesis by forebears we can never know.
Our inheritance includes both their achievements and their failures, the good they did, as well as the wrongs. History can be hard to compass, viewed as it is through the prism of time, which can both clarifying and distorting.
And yet its consequences resonate with contemporary force.
He starts by saying he and the Queen are delighted to attend this 28th Chogm.
He says he has been attending these meetings for almost 30 years.
It is even more sobering to think that 30 years ago, most people had never bought anything online. Many had never sent an email, and connecting to the web involved a rather alarming series of screeches from a telephone line.
In fact, in those days, the internet was so new people referred to it as the information superhighway.
I suspect that 30 years later, many of those early users, some in this room perhaps, are still trying to remember their first passwords.
Sunder Katwala is also one of the experts questioning the idea that Shabana Mahmood’s care workers U-turn will lead to the government missing out on a chunk of savings worth £10bn – because, he says, those savings never existed anyway. He says:
Minister does not contest inaccurate/untrue claim about impacts of government policy: there was no saving of billions under the original plan at all. It was a government-created myth that has bounced back
This debate is ridiculous. The £10 bn figure should have been zero. The loss of deterred workers who would be net contributors will be similar under the new proposal. And either way, punitive, retrospective rule-changes are tools of illiberal governments.
As explained here, the Home Office justifed its £10bn figure in a document it published earlier this year. The IPPR published a critique of it yesterday.
Earlier this year, Jonathan Portes, a professor of economics and public policy at King’s College London, produced his own analysis saying that the ILR proposals Mahmood published in November last year would save just £600m.
Back to Kemi Badenoch’s announcement about ILR (see 2.16pm), and Sunder Katwala from the British Future thinktank argues that she has changed her tune on retrospective legislation.
“We have a principle. We don’t believe in making things retrospective” - Kemi Badenoch, 30th October 2025
“If somebody is granted ILR by the Labour govt, and not a net contributor, we would review and stop their ILR”, - Kemi Badenoch, 3rd November 2026
Gaston Browne, the prime minister of Antigua and Barbuda, is speaking now at the Chogm opening ceremony, where he is the host.
He says this could be a particularly consequential summit.
He goes on:
There are some who question whether or not the Commonwealth remains relevant. Our answer must not rest on history or sentiment alone. It must be demonstrated through results in the opportunities we create, the partnerships reforge, and the tangible improvements we deliver in the lives of our people.
Badenoch says Tories would remove ILR concession for care workers announced by Shabana Mahmood
Kemi Badenoch has signalled that, if the Conservatives win the next election, they will remove the indefinite leave to remain concession for care workers announced by Shabana Mahmood yesterday. In a post on social media, she said:
Shabana has made a serious mistake surrendering to Labour MPs. So I’m putting people on notice - when we get into government we will scrap this weak policy.
Immigration is too high. Labour are making a bad situation much, much worse.
The policy announced yesterday actually significantly tightens ILR rules, compared to what they say now, but by “weak policy”, Badenoch is referring to the concessions. She makes this clear in a video she has posted setting out her policy.

בנאומו בפתיחת כינוס ראשי ממשלות חבר העמים הבריטי באנטיגואה, הצהיר המלך צ'ארלס כי היסטוריית סחר העבדים מעוררת בו חלחלה עמוקה ותחושת צער אישית. עם זאת, הוא נמנע מהוצאת התנצלות רשמית והדגיש את החשיבות של התמודדות עם עוולות העבר באמצעות שיתופי פעולה עתידיים בחינוך, בכלכלה ובאקלים.

בנושא פוליטי פנימי, ועדת התקנים והנהלים בפרלמנט הסקוטי קראה לבחון מחדש את החוק המאפשר לתושבי חוץ בעלי מעמד זמני להתמודד בבחירות לפרלמנט ולרשויות המקומיות. ההמלצה הגיעה בעקבות ביקורת ציבורית על בחירתו של סטודנט בעל ויזה זמנית למשרה פרלמנטרית.

בנוסף, ראש עיריית מנצ'סטר לשעבר אנדי ברנהם הצהיר כי הוא מייחס חשיבות פחותה לביקורת עיתונאית בהשוואה לראשי ממשלה קודמים, וכי הוא מעדיף לתת עדיפות לתקשורת ישירה דרך הרשתות החברתיות.
